title: Work as practice
hook: the Buddha taught farmers, traders, kings and servants where they were
tomorrow: what makes a job honest: what you sell, or how you sell it?

segments.voice: Yesterday the ten perfections closed, and one of them is next for you. Now a new stretch begins, the householder's path, starting where most of the day goes: work.

On a new job, someone always asks what you actually do all day. A farmer once put that question to the Buddha. It's sowing season. A brahmin named Bharadvaja has his plows out in the field, and food is being handed out to the workers. The Buddha walks up with his bowl and stands there. The farmer looks him over. I plow and sow, he says, and when I've plowed and sown, I eat. You should plow and sow too, and then eat. A fair point, from a man with dirt on his hands. And the Buddha says: I too plow and sow, and then I eat. The farmer squints. I don't see your yoke, or your plow, or your ox.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU DO ALL DAY?` → `SOWING SEASON.` → `I PLOW AND SOW. DO YOU?` → `I TOO PLOW AND SOW.`

segments.voice: So the Buddha answers in the farmer's own language. Faith is the seed, he says. Discipline is the rain. Wisdom is my yoke and plow. Conscience is the pole, the mind is the strap, mindfulness my plowshare and goad. Effort is my ox, pulling toward freedom without turning back. That's the whole move. He doesn't drag the farmer out of the field to teach him. He walks into the field and teaches in plows and oxen. And it cuts the other way too. If the path can be described as farming, a farmer's day can carry the path. The plowshare is mindfulness. The straight furrow is attention that doesn't wander off. Work as practice doesn't mean quitting your job for a temple. It means the barista, the nurse, the coder and the mat cutter bring the same tools to the task in front of them: a steady mind, honest effort, attention on the next cut. One more detail. The farmer is so moved that he offers a big bowl of milk-rice. The Buddha declines it. He won't take food earned by reciting verses. Even in the field, he keeps the teaching from becoming a sale.
screen: `FAITH THE SEED, WISDOM THE PLOW.` · `HE TEACHES IN THE FARMER'S FIELD.` · `THE SAME TOOLS, ANY JOB.` · `HE DECLINES THE MILK-RICE.` · then, large: `WHERE YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: Pick up one small task within reach: fold a blanket, wipe a screen, line up the pens. Do only that, slowly, with your whole attention on your hands, like a furrow you're keeping straight. When the mind wanders off, bring it back to the hands.
Work as practice: bringing the path's tools, mindfulness, effort and a steady mind, to the work in front of you.
Keep this one: where you are, in the field you're already standing in. One of fifty, and the new stretch has begun.

screen: `DAY 1576 COUNTS.` → `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH · 1 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT MAKES A JOB HONEST?`

howItsDone: In Zen monasteries, daily work such as cooking and cleaning (samu) is treated as practice, and lay Buddhists bring mindfulness to their jobs in the same spirit.

fork.setup: your friend is a barista and says her job is "just making coffee," nothing spiritual. what fits work as practice?
options: each cup can get her full attention; the job itself can carry practice.
she should find a calmer job first, and start practicing after that.

fork.reveal: the Buddha met a farmer in his own field and described his practice as plowing. the work in front of you can carry the path.

original.note: Pali: kasi, plowing or farming, as in the farmer's name in the sutta, Kasibharadvaja.

trapdoor: what you thought: practice is something you do after work.
what it means: the path's tools go to work with you: a steady mind, effort, attention on the next task.
what a scholar hears: the Kasibharadvaja Sutta (Sutta Nipata 1.4; also SN 7.11) has the Buddha answer a farmer in farming terms: faith the seed, mindfulness the plowshare and goad.

leaving your job to live in a monastery
working extra hours as a kind of offering

chat.says: petrov made it official: i'm hired! but cutting mats all day isn't exactly "practice"... right?
options: It can be. The Buddha told a farmer he plows too. Bring mindfulness to each cut.
Not really. Real practice happens on the cushion, after your shift is over.
Only if the work is spiritual, like temple posters or teaching meditation.
chat.meaning: The Buddha described his practice as plowing and met the farmer in his own field. Work done with mindfulness and effort can be practice, where you are.

tie.story: When a farmer told the Buddha to plow and sow, the Buddha said he does: faith the seed, mindfulness the plowshare.
tie.friend: Mai can make each mat cut a straight furrow: a steady mind and honest effort.

Bharadvaja.meaning: the brahmin farmer who questions the Buddha

brahmin.meaning: a member of the priestly class in ancient India

milk-rice.meaning: rice cooked in milk, a rich food to offer
